CausalChain: Chronic HBV/HCV and inflammatory stimuli -> Elevated IL-6 secretion -> IL-6 binds IL-6R on hepatocytes -> Activation of JAK leading to STAT3 phosphorylation -> STAT3 translocates to nucleus and induces AFP expression and EMT transcription factors -> Increased AFP secretion reinforces IL-6 production and sustains STAT3 activation -> Amplification of LCSC formation, EMT, and immune suppression -> Enhanced drug resistance and tumor progression
Hypothesis: In HCC, STAT3‐mediated upregulation of AFP establishes a positive feedback loop that amplifies IL-6 signaling, promotes the formation of cancer stem cells and facilitates immune escape; thus, targeting the AFP-STAT3 interaction may disrupt this feed‐forward mechanism and overcome drug resistance and tumor progression.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by an inflammatory microenvironment in which the IL‐6/STAT3 axis plays a central role, not only by driving classical oncogenic processes such as proliferation, survival and immune evasion, but also by inducing the expression of alpha‐fetoprotein (AFP). Emerging evidence suggests that AFP, beyond serving as a biomarker for HCC, may participate in reinforcing the IL‐6/STAT3 signaling cascade through a positive feedback loop. In this hypothesis, we propose that chronic inflammatory stimuli—such as those resulting from HBV/HCV infection—lead to increased secretion of IL‐6, driving STAT3 phosphorylation and nuclear translocation. Activated STAT3 then upregulates genes including AFP and key EMT transcription factors, which further promote IL‐6 secretion, hepatocellular transformation and enrichment of liver cancer stem cells (LCSCs). This self‐reinforcing loop may contribute to enhanced drug resistance and immune escape. Intervening at the level of the AFP‐STAT3 interaction, or disrupting the resultant epigenetic programming in tumor and stromal cells, might offer a novel approach to break this feedback circuit and improve the therapeutic outcomes in HCC.
